Hi Mina,

Thanks again for the demo last week. We have an internal kickoff tomorrow to align procurement with engineering and wanted a quick sizing sanity check before we finalize the RFP. Highcrest plans to reserve dedicated capacity for two main workloads:

- "Compose" (long-context generation, often >8k tokens, uses a 70B model).
- "EmbedServe" (shorter queries, high QPS for semantic search, uses 3B embedding model).

Primary concerns: memory footprint for large KV cache, peak p95 latency under 200ms for Compose at small burst scale, and predictable unit economics for reserved capacity. Our initial preference is to mix L4 for EmbedServe and either A100 or H100 for Compose, but engineering asked us to validate whether we should standardize on one SKU or mix and match.

Can you provide a recommendation and a quick rationale (H100 vs A100 vs L4) plus any fallback strategy we should include in the contract (e.g., automatic fallthrough to hosted variant or cross-region failover)? We also attached a rough query profile (highcrest-query-profile.csv).

Appreciate any quick guidance — procurement is trying to lock targets by Wednesday.

Thanks,

Tom / team —

High-level recommendation (TL;DR):
- Use a mixed fleet: H100 (for Compose / long-context heavy instances) + L4 (for EmbedServe). Avoid A100 unless you have existing A100 inventory or specific FP16 kernel dependencies.

Rationale and tradeoffs:
- H100: best raw perf on dense, long-context autoregressive workloads and superior attention/kv throughput for >8k sequences. Provides the headroom to keep p95 < 200ms with aggressive batching and KV cache pinned in GPU memory. Downside: higher cost per GPU and fewer seats per rack; still the safest choice if latency SLOs are firm.

- A100: solid general-purpose GPU for many transformer workloads and lower unit cost than H100 in many clouds, but its attention perf and memory bandwidth lag H100 for large KV-intensive inference. If Compose latency SLOs are soft or you plan to heavily quantize/partition KV cache, A100 can be OK.

- L4: optimal for embeddings/short-context low-memory models. Very cost-effective for high QPS. Use L4 pool behind the same routing policy and autoscale it aggressively for bursty search traffic.

Sizing heuristics (based on your CSV + Redwood defaults):
- Compose workload: assuming 70B model quantized to 4-bit-ish profile and 10% of requests are >=8k tokens, expected steady concurrency 40 sessions, p95 tokens/sec ~120. Plan for 6 H100 nodes (or equivalent H100 time-slices) to meet p95 headroom with continuous batching + prefix cache. That maps to ~3 full racks if you want redundancy + canary.

- EmbedServe: expected steady QPS 1.5k with short payloads; L4 pool of 8-12 GPUs with autoscale should cover p99 latency target and keep cost per embed low.

Fallback & contract clauses to include:
- Cross-SKU fallthrough: automated routing to a compatible model variant on alternate SKU (A100 or H100 hosted fallback) when dedicated pool is saturated.
- Cache warming and prefix prefetch policy for predictable p95 during predictable bursts.
- Burst capacity credits: include X hours of hosted-burst to handle structured product launches.

Attachments included: sku-fitment-matrix.xlsx (contains cost-per-token estimates, rack counts, and stress test results) and a short mutual action plan (mutual_action_plan_highcrest.md).

Next steps (proposed):
1) We validate steady/peak concurrency numbers with your Cloud Ops (Tom / cloudops).
2) Redwood drafts a 1-page MAM + rough pricing for dedicated pool + optional hosted-burst.
3) Marissa will set up a 30-min technical alignment call with your infra leads.

Notes on A100 vs H100 decision boundary:
- If Highcrest values latency predictability under high-long-context mix and plans to run few large models, pick H100.
- If cost containment and capacity density are primary, and you can accept higher p95 variability or plan to shard models, A100 is a compromise.

Happy to walk through the SKU-fit matrix live — I built the attached spreadsheet to show marginal cost per p95-ms improvement so procurement can see the delta.
